Subject: Renewal planning — pricing lock / staged prepay options

Marcus —

Hope you’re well. Our renewal for the Redwood contract comes up at the end of Q3 and finance is pushing to lock pricing for FY27. Two asks from our side:

1) Can Redwood provide a multi-year prepay option that lets us lock year-over-year unit pricing? We’re open to a 2–3 year term.
2) We have seasonal usage — a steady ramp in H1 then spike in Q4. Would you support a staged prepay (partial prepay up front + scheduled top-ups) so we don’t overcommit cash early?

Attached is our current usage trend and a simple forecast (see BlueCrest_Prepay_Scenarios.xlsx). We need a commercial outline by early June to present internally.

Samira —

Really appreciate the heads-up and the forecast. Short answer: yes, we can do a multi-year price lock and we commonly support staged prepay structures for customers with variable usage.

High-level options I propose for your internal review:

- Option A — 2-year prepay (pay 100% up front): 15% term discount, price locked for 24 months.
- Option B — 3-year prepay with staging: 10% upfront on Year 1 (to cover base capacity), then two scheduled top-ups at 12 and 24 months. Price lock across all three years; top-ups billed at the discounted rate but collected on scheduled dates.
- Option C — Annual prepay ladder: 12% discount if you commit to annual prepay each year in advance (renewable). Allows you to keep cash flow aligned with usage.

I’ve looped in Monica (Finance approvals) and Rishi (Sales leadership) to confirm commercial flexibility and the ramp schedule mechanics. If you can confirm target term (2 vs 3 years) and a preferred cash cadence, I’ll get a formal term sheet out this week.

Best,
Marcus Lin
Account Executive — Enterprise
Redwood Inference

Marcus —

Thanks for flagging. Finance perspective:

- 15% for a 2-year full prepay is within policy but needs VP Ops
  approval if ARR > $1.2M. Please confirm expected ARR under the commit.
- For staged prepay we prefer a single committed contract with scheduled invoices (top-ups) rather than multiple SKUs — reduces reconciliation overhead and preserves the locked unit price.
- Refunds: we generally do not offer cash refunds for unused prepay; unused credit rolls forward for 12 months with an option to convert to lower-tier credits after that. We should put that in term language.

Recommend we present Option B (3-year staged) as the primary path — it preserves cash flexibility for the customer and reduces our revenue recognition complexity. Suggest commercial language: 10% term discount on committed dollars; scheduled top-ups at month 12 and month 24; price locked across the term; rollover window of 12 months for unused credits.

Marking as +1 from Finance but will need Rishi / Sales sign-off on levels.

-Monica
Director, Finance Partnerships
Redwood Inference

Samira / Tom —

Thanks again for the data. Per our internal alignment (Monica + Rishi), here is the formal proposal we recommend for your internal review:

Summary: 3-year staged prepay to lock unit pricing while allowing scheduled cash top-ups.

Key terms (summary):
- Term: 36 months (2027–2029)
- Commitment structure: Year 1 upfront payment = 35% of first-year committed dollars (covers baseline capacity). Scheduled top-ups at month 12 (25% of year 2 committed $) and month 24 (40% of year 3 committed $) — schedule can be adjusted to match your forecast.
- Discount: 10% on committed dollars for the entire 3-year period (applies to both upfront and top-up invoices).
- Price lock: unit pricing locked for 36 months. Any additional overage usage billed at standard list price.
- Rollover: Unused prepaid credits roll forward up to 12 months; after 12 months credits may be converted to service credits only.
- Approval: Subject to a Master Order Amendment and VP Ops approval for discounts >10% for deals over $1.2M.

Attachments: Redwood_MultiYear_Term_Sheet_v2.pdf (detailed term sheet), MOA template.

Next steps: If acceptable, sign the MOA and we’ll route for internal approvals and DocuSign. If you’d like, I can model a cash-flow schedule against your forecast and adjust the top-up cadence.

Best,
Marcus Lin
Account Executive — Enterprise
